title: International Organisations
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about how nations cooperate across borders -- the United Nations, regional bodies, and the institutions of global governance built after the Second World War.
competenceGoals: explore and discuss how international organisations contribute to global cooperation and governance
analyse the role of multilateral institutions in addressing transnational challenges

content.content:
## No country can do it alone

Climate change, pandemics, terrorism, economic instability -- the biggest problems of our age have one thing in common: none of them respect national borders, and none can be solved by a single country acting alone. **International organisations** provide the frameworks and institutions through which states work together on these shared challenges.

The modern system of international organisations was built largely after the devastation of the Second World War. Leaders had seen how unchecked nationalism and the absence of effective cooperation helped produce two catastrophic global conflicts within a single generation. The answer was a new architecture of global governance, centred on the United Nations but reaching out to a wide range of specialised agencies and regional bodies. Today there are hundreds of international organisations shaping everything from trade policy to human rights standards. Understanding how they work -- and where they fall short -- is essential for making sense of contemporary international relations.

## The United Nations and its powers

At the centre stands the **United Nations (UN)**, founded in 1945 with 51 member states and now numbering 193. Its purposes, set out in the UN Charter, are to maintain international peace and security, develop friendly relations among nations, achieve cooperation on economic, social and humanitarian issues, and promote respect for human rights. The UN works through several key organs. The *General Assembly* gives every member one vote and discusses and recommends on global issues. The *Security Council* has 15 members -- including five permanent members with veto power: the USA, UK, France, Russia and China -- and bears responsibility for peace and security. The *Secretariat* is the administrative arm, led by the Secretary-General, and the *International Court of Justice* settles legal disputes between states. Crucially, the UN has no army of its own and no power to tax, so its effectiveness depends on the willingness of member states, especially the major powers, to cooperate.

One of the UN's most visible roles is peacekeeping. Since 1948 it has deployed over 70 peacekeeping operations, typically involving soldiers from many member states wearing the UN's distinctive blue helmets. Peacekeepers are not sent to fight wars; they monitor ceasefires, protect civilians and help build conditions for lasting peace, with successes in Mozambique, East Timor and Sierra Leone. But an honest account must include the failures too. In Rwanda in 1994, a small UN force was unable to prevent genocide, and in Srebrenica in 1995, Dutch peacekeepers failed to protect Bosnian Muslims from massacre. These tragedies raised hard questions about when and how the international community should intervene. The *veto power* of the five permanent members is itself a defining and controversial feature: it can block action even in the face of grave crises, which some defend as keeping the major powers engaged and others criticise as paralysing the Council -- a debate worth presenting fairly rather than taking a side on.

content.content:
## Beyond the UN: regional cooperation

Global bodies like the UN are not the whole story. Numerous **regional organisations** play significant roles in international relations, often allowing states with geographic proximity and shared interests to cooperate more effectively than they could through global institutions alone. The **European Union (EU)** is a supranational organisation of 27 European states with shared institutions, a common market and a single currency, the euro, used by most members; notably, it can pass laws that are binding on member states. **NATO**, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, is a military alliance of 32 states in North America and Europe, built on the principle in Article 5 that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The **African Union** is a continental organisation of 55 African states promoting political and economic integration, and **ASEAN**, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, is a regional bloc of 10 states focused on economic cooperation and stability.

These organisations illustrate two important distinctions in how states cooperate. The first is between *intergovernmental* and *supranational* bodies. Most international organisations are intergovernmental, meaning states cooperate while keeping their sovereignty -- the UN works this way. But some, like the EU, are supranational, meaning their authority can transcend and bind member states, who pool some of their sovereignty for shared benefit. This trade-off is central to debates about international cooperation: pooling sovereignty can enable more effective collective action but raises questions about democratic control. The second distinction concerns *multilateralism* -- cooperation among multiple states through institutions -- which is the basic principle underlying the whole system. The structure of these organisations affects how responsive they are, how power is checked, and how citizens experience the reach of international governance in their daily lives. The picture that emerges is of a layered system, with global, regional and specialised bodies each playing a part in helping sovereign states address problems too big for any one of them.

exercise.task: Test yourself on regional organisations and global governance:

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: What is distinctive about the European Union as an organisation?

options.text: It has no shared institutions
It is only a military alliance
It has no common currency
It is supranational and can pass laws binding on member states

questions.solution: The EU is a supranational organisation that can pass laws binding on its member states, who pool some of their sovereignty, with a common market and the euro.

questions.task: What is the core principle of NATO under Article 5?

options.text: That an attack on one member is considered an attack on all
That all members share a currency
That members must adopt the same laws
That members cannot trade with each other

questions.solution: NATO's Article 5 establishes that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all, the core of the collective-defence alliance.

questions.task: What is the difference between intergovernmental and supranational organisations?

options.text: They are identical
Intergovernmental bodies preserve sovereignty; supranational bodies can bind members
Supranational bodies have no power
Intergovernmental bodies always have an army

questions.solution: In intergovernmental bodies like the UN, states cooperate while keeping their sovereignty; in supranational bodies like the EU, authority can transcend and bind member states.

options.text: One country acting alone
A type of currency
Cooperation among multiple states through institutions
A military invasion

questions.solution: Multilateralism is cooperation among multiple states through institutions, the basic principle underlying the system of international organisations.

content.content:
## In short

Because the great challenges of our age cross borders, international organisations provide frameworks for states to cooperate, an architecture built largely after the Second World War. At its centre is the United Nations, with 193 members and key organs including the General Assembly and the Security Council, whose five permanent members hold a defining and controversial veto power. The UN has no army or taxing power, so it depends on member states' cooperation, and its peacekeeping record includes both successes and failures like Rwanda and Srebrenica. Regional organisations such as the EU, NATO, the African Union and ASEAN add further layers, illustrating the distinction between intergovernmental cooperation and the supranational pooling of sovereignty. The result is a layered system of multilateralism through which sovereign states tackle problems too big to face alone.
